title: How to Build an IB Psychology Study Group
summary: Build an IB Psychology study group that stays focused from September to November with clear roles, active recall, exam practice, and weekly plans.
body_markdown:
An **IB Psychology study group** works when every meeting produces evidence of learning, such as recalled content, corrected answers, essay plans, research-method analysis, or timed responses. It fails when members arrive unprepared and spend the session rereading notes.


For September to November, form a group of **3-5 dependable students** , meet consistently, rotate roles, and prioritize individual retrieval followed by structured discussion. This system can work for both SL and HL students.


### Check which IB Psychology course you are studying


Confirm your assessment route with your teacher before selecting resources. The previous Psychology course has its **last assessment in 2026** , while the revised course has its **first assessment in 2027** , as explained on the[official IB Psychology page](https://www.ibo.org/programmes/diploma-programme/curriculum/individuals-and-societies/psychology/) .


Under the revised course, Paper 1 integrates concepts, content, and contexts. Paper 2 assesses research methodology and class practicals, while HL students also complete a data-analysis Paper 3. The internal assessment is a research proposal, according to the[official Psychology subject brief](https://ibo.org/globalassets/new-structure/programmes/dp/pdfs/dp_psychology_subjectbrief_en.pdf) .


A group preparing for November 2026 may still follow the earlier course. Do not combine materials from both routes unless your teacher confirms their relevance.


### Form an accountable group


Choose members for reliability rather than friendship alone. Students should follow the same assessment route, meet regularly, and attempt questions before seeing answers.


At the first meeting, agree on:


- A weekly meeting of **60-90 minutes**
- The meeting location or online platform
- Required preparation
- Independent attempts before discussion
- Procedures for absences and repeated missed work


Three to five members provide varied interpretations without allowing quieter students to disappear.


### Build a shared syllabus map


Before assigning topics, turn the relevant syllabus or subject brief into a checklist. Record each concept, content area, context, research-methods skill, class practical, and assessment task that your class must cover. Mark every item red, amber, or green individually before combining results; a group average can hide one student's serious gap.


Use the map to choose weekly priorities. Red items need direct teaching, retrieval, and a short exam task; amber items need application and feedback; green items need occasional spaced retesting. Keep ownership shared rather than permanently assigning one member the biological approach and another research methods, because each student must be able to answer independently.


### Give every meeting a visible structure


Begin with closed-book work. Research on the[science of learning](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5780548/) supports retrieval practice and spacing over passive rereading. Research into[collaborative retrieval practice](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10929687/) also suggests that structured group recall can support later individual memory.


Use this **75-minute agenda** :


Time Activity Required output


0-10 minutes Closed-book retrieval Definitions, study details, or a concept map


10-25 minutes Compare and correct Verified correction list


25-45 minutes Application task Scenario response, analysis, or essay plan


45-65 minutes Timed individual writing One response from every member


65-75 minutes Feedback Error-log entries and new assignments


Everyone should write before anyone speaks. Otherwise, students may merely recognize a confident member's answer instead of retrieving the information themselves.


### Rotate study-group roles


Assign and rotate these roles weekly:


- **Facilitator:** follows the agenda and redirects unrelated discussion.
- **Question setter:** prepares 5-8 retrieval and application questions.
- **Evidence checker:** verifies definitions, research details, and conclusions.
- **Examiner:** checks command terms and relevance.
- **Recorder:** updates the error log and next-session plan.


When correcting an answer, identify the disputed point, check an approved source, and record the accurate version. This prevents the group from reinforcing incorrect study details or exaggerated conclusions.


### Use Psychology-specific activities


For each study, theory, or model, create a compact record containing its topic, aim, essential method, relevant findings, justified conclusion, methodological limitations, ethical issues, and possible applications. One member can explain it from memory while the others independently record omissions.


Practise applying knowledge to unfamiliar situations. For example, when considering school phone restrictions, students might apply cognitive load, conformity, social identity, motivation, or research-design concepts. Explain why the concept fits, what evidence supports it, and where the explanation is limited.


Include research methods every week. Compare experiments and correlational studies, identify sampling problems, evaluate operationalization, distinguish correlation from causation, and suggest ethical improvements. Revised-course students should revisit class practicals because Paper 2 explicitly assesses them.


### Run a complete practice cycle


Choose one unfamiliar prompt and give every member five minutes to plan silently. Compare thesis statements, relevant evidence, and possible limitations, then agree on what a strong response requires without copying one model answer. Each student should next write a paragraph or response independently under a realistic time limit.


Exchange responses and give one specific strength, one correction, and one priority for revision. The writer then improves the answer from memory instead of merely reading the comments. This sequence moves from retrieval to discussion, individual performance, feedback, and immediate correction, making the meeting more useful than shared note-taking.


The[IB Psychology research-methods resources](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-psychology-new/ib-psychology-new-24-research-methodology) and[research-methodology Questionbank](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-psychology-new/ib-psychology-new-24-research-methodology/questionbank) provide terminology and practice prompts.


### Follow a September-to-November plan


Period Priority Group output


September weeks 1-2 Diagnose weaknesses Contract, topic audit, baseline response


September weeks 3-4 Secure core knowledge Evidence bank and retrieval quizzes


October weeks 1-2 Apply knowledge Scenario responses and comparisons


October weeks 3-4 Strengthen evaluation Critiques, redesigns, and essay plans


November weeks 1-2 Increase timed work Individual responses and peer feedback


November weeks 3-4 Repair weaknesses Retests and a cumulative mini-mock


This plan uses **spacing** by revisiting topics after delays and **interleaving** by mixing concepts, contexts, evidence, and methods.


### Keep feedback accurate


Peer feedback should ask whether the response addresses the command term, explains Psychology accurately, and uses evidence that supports its claim. Maintain an error log recording the question, error, corrected understanding, and retest date. Revisit weaknesses after one or two weeks.


Choose the correct[RevisionDojo IB Psychology pathway](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/revisiondojo-ib-psychology-coverage) . Use either the[Questionbank for assessment through 2026](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-psychology/questionbank) or the[first-exam-2027 Questionbank](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-psychology-new/questionbank) .


Avoid shared rereading, permanent division of topics, unchecked factual debates, and meetings dominated by one student. Every session needs independent writing because IB assessment remains individual.


### Measure whether the group is working


Review the group after three or four meetings. Useful indicators include improved closed-book quiz scores, fewer repeated errors, more complete timed answers, and greater confidence applying evidence to unfamiliar prompts. Attendance alone does not demonstrate that the meetings are effective.


Ask each member which activity produces the clearest improvement and which wastes time. Adjust the agenda using this evidence, but keep retrieval and individual writing. If performance remains unchanged, reduce the amount of discussion, verify resource quality, and assign narrower preparation tasks before adding longer meetings.


### Conclusion


An effective IB Psychology study group is small, consistent, and organized around retrieval, application, feedback, and retesting. RevisionDojo Study Notes or Flashcards can support preparation, while the Questionbank and Jojo AI can help identify weaknesses after timed practice.
